PART B2
Read Text 5 and answer questions 43–64 in the Question-Answer Book for Part B2.
Quiet Quitting
[1] Quiet quitting is a buzzy term doing the rounds today. In fact, a Google search
produces hits from The Washington Post, The New York Times, The Wall Street
Journal, and countless academic publications. At this moment, at least 50% of the
North American workforce is engaged in a wave of disengagement dubbed quiet
quitting. But what does it mean and how will it impact university graduates as they
prepare to embark on 21st-century careers?
What is quiet quitting?
[2] As many have noted the term itself is misleading. No, it does not refer to wordlessly
slipping out the door or logging out of the group chat without so much as a peace sign
emoji. Nor does it mean an employee permanently abandoning their post. Quiet
quitters believe a more accurate way to describe this is working your contract or acting
your wage. Carrie Bulger, PhD, a professor of organizational psychology, defines quiet
quitting as a “renewed effort to really focus on what a job is and isn’t.”
[3] No matter what terminology we use, quiet quitting is less a harbinger of widespread
revolt and more of a long overdue reckoning with outdated practices and stale office
culture. “For some people, it’s probably a sign of dissatisfaction and a sign that they’re
going to leave,” Bulger said. “But I think for others, it’s something else.”
[4] Being forced to work at home amid the tumult of 2020 was an eye-opening
experience, one that emboldened even the most dedicated employees to set healthy
boundaries. And enforcing those boundaries can appear, through the lens of leadership,
like slacking. “But it is quite possible to be invested in your work and redirect that
passion once you clock out for the day. Pursuing work-life enrichment prioritizes
self-care in one area and tends to breed success in the other,” Bulger said.

Going against the grind
[5] The signs are all around us — productivity is no longer seen as the badge of honor it
once was, and Generation Z are starting to question how relevant it is while seeking
better frameworks that support the kind of life they want to live. Launched in 2013, one
online community that exists for people who ‘want help with their own work-life related
struggles’ saw an upsurge in followers in late 2021. The Instagram account The Nap
Ministry has a similar popularity arc and saw a huge explosion of followers since the
start of the pandemic, numbering in the tens of thousands per day. Tricia Hersey, its
creator, believes Gen Z work harder; they just don’t want to live to work. To her, and to
many others, it is about ‘not running ourselves into the ground.’
[6] Quiet quitting is only one note in this growing chorus, and we should be careful not
to dismiss it as just another trend or a singular occurrence. Instead, we should step back
and look at the whole picture and what that means for the way we’ve been working and
how we should move forward.
[7] There are, of course, divergent perspectives on quiet quitting. There’s what it means
for workers and what it means for panicked employers in a precarious economy, and the
collision of those viewpoints can have drastic consequences for the former. Writing for
The Wall Street Journal, columnist Callum Borchers outlined the perils of quiet
quitting. Borchers has encountered a new term quiet firing in which reputations suffer
as a result of perceived apathy; responsibilities are gradually diminished and a path
toward actual termination materializes. “Companies have always had subtle ways to
nudge people out the door,” Borchers said. “Tactics include sidelining them by cutting
responsibilities or denying promotions and raises to make someone miserable enough to
leave.”

[8] Gergo Vari, CEO of online job searching platform Lensa, also believes the decision
won’t serve employees long-term either. “Anytime that you silence your own voice in an
organization, you may be depriving yourself of the opportunity to change that
organization.” Stepping away from hustle culture can also cause tension between
employees and may result in a rift between fellow colleagues who may have to pick up
the slack. “If people feel like their co-workers aren’t committed to quality work there can
be friction inside teams and organizations.”
A generational divide
[9] Today’s college students are rightly praised for their resiliency. But the same skills
that made them so adaptable during the pandemic — they are digital natives who prefer
Zoom lectures to the real thing — make them the target of generational disdain once
they enter the workforce. Can’t you just hear the grumbling: “We wouldn’t have to
worry about quiet quitting if these kids would get off TikTok and do their jobs.
Fittingly, the movement’s origins can be traced to TikTok, the massively popular
video-sharing app, where the influencer Zaid Khan uttered a phrase that’s been quoted
in countless news articles: “Your worth as a person is not defined by your labor.”
[10] In an essay for The New Yorker, Cal Newport, an associate professor of computer
science, posits that Gen Z is better equipped than its forebears to leverage technology to
push back against workplace norms. Gen Z enters the workforce with “a mindset that is
notably distinct from the millennials who preceded them,” Newport writes. As the first
group to fully come of age with smartphones and social media, Gen Z “formed an
understanding of the world in which the boundaries between the digital and real are
blurred.” They have so thoroughly mixed work and self, the suffocating grimness of
modern office life hits a more personal level and it has become clear to many that they
need to separate their personhood from their jobs.

[11] Work, of course, remains essential within our current economic and social
environment and trends like quiet quitting are inevitable during times of greater
upheaval. What we need to do is take a step back and take a critical look at how we can
adapt the way we work to suit our current context while promoting a more modern and
balanced way of life. As Barnaby Lashbrooke wrote in Forbes: “Of course we have to
work: to put a roof overhead and food on the table. But life should come first, and work
should be the enabler.”

slacking.
而當員工開始維護這些界線時，從管理階層的角度看來，這可能會像是在偷
懶。

“But it is quite possible to be invested in your work and redirect that passion
once you clock out for the day.

的生活面向。

New concept
Borchers has encountered a new term quiet firing in which reputations suffer as
a result of perceived apathy; responsibilities are gradually diminished and a path
toward actual termination materializes.

“Companies have always had subtle ways to nudge people out the door,”
Borchers said.

Example
“Tactics include sidelining them by cutting responsibilities or denying
promotions and raises to make someone miserable enough to leave.”
「這些手段包括把人邊緣化、削減其職責，或者拒絕升遷與加薪，好讓對方痛
苦到自己離開。」

Topic Sentence

今天的大學生確實理應因為他們的韌性而受到稱讚。
Contrast
But the same skills that made them so adaptable during the pandemic — they
are digital natives who prefer Zoom lectures to the real thing — make them the
target of generational disdain once they enter the workforce.
但正是那些讓他們在疫情期間顯得如此適應力強的特質——例如作為數位
原生代，更喜歡 Zoom 課堂而不是實體課——在他們進入職場後，也使他們
成為世代偏見與不滿的目標。

Can’t you just hear the grumbling: “We wouldn’t have to worry about quiet
quitting if these kids would get off TikTok and do their jobs.”

就不用擔心 quiet quitting 了。」

computer science, posits that Gen Z is better equipped than its forebears to
leverage technology to push back against workplace norms.

Gen Z enters the workforce with “a mindset that is notably distinct from the
millennials who preceded them,” Newport writes.
Newport 寫道，Z 世代進入職場時所帶著的「思維模式，與在他們之前的千禧
世代明顯不同」。
Background / Explanation
As the first group to fully come of age with smartphones and social media, Gen
Z “formed an understanding of the world in which the boundaries between the
digital and real are blurred.”
作為第一個在智慧型手機與社群媒體環境中完整成長起來的世代，Z 世代
「形成了一種對世界的理解：數位與現實之間的界線是模糊的」。

Balanced conclusion
Work, of course, remains essential within our current economic and social
environment and trends like quiet quitting are inevitable during times of
greater upheaval.
當然，在當前的經濟與社會環境中，工作依然是必要的，而像 quiet quitting 這
樣的趨勢，在動盪加劇的時代裡也是難以避免的。
Recommendation
What we need to do is take a step back and take a critical look at how we can
adapt the way we work to suit our current context while promoting a more
modern and balanced way of life.
我們需要做的，是退一步，以批判性的眼光檢視：我們該如何調整工作方式，
去配合當下的處境，同時推動一種更現代、更平衡的生活方式。
Final quote / takeaway
As Barnaby Lashbrooke wrote in Forbes: “Of course we have to work: to put a
roof overhead and food on the table. But life should come first, and work should
be the enabler.”

有屋頂遮頭，也要有食物上桌。但人生應該排在第一位，而工作應該只是讓
人生得以實現的工具。」

為甚麼這一格不能只答「not talking」？
很多學生會把 (i) 寫得太短，例如：
● not talking
● not saying anything
● not making noise

但答得還不夠成熟、精準
因為 passage 裡的 [quiet] 不是單純指「安靜」的聲音狀態，
而是指一種更完整的 無聲離開 / 不出聲退出 的印象。
也就是說，這一格真正的核心是：
● leaving silently
● wordlessly slipping out
● disappearing without saying anything
所以最穩陣的英文答案應該是：
● It does not mean leaving silently / wordlessly.
而不是只寫：
● quiet = not speaking

● [But it is quite possible to be invested in your work and redirect that

這句裡，和題目最直接對應的，當然是：
● [clock out for the day]

這裡的 [once you clock out for the day] 很明顯是在標示：
工作時間結束的那一刻

[work-life enrichment] 這個 phrase 本身就很重要。
它不是 saying:
● work versus life
● work or life
● work takes away from life
而是：
life and work can enrich each other
也就是說：
● 當你在生活那邊照顧好自己
● 反而能提升工作那邊的表現
這就解釋了為甚麼 [self-care] 在其中一邊， 而 [success] 在另一邊。
不是因為兩邊毫無關係， 反而正正因為兩邊互相影響
所以這一題背後的 deeper meaning 是：
自我照顧不是工作投入的敵人，
而可能是工作成功的來源之一。
而這個 deeper meaning，也進一步支持：
● one area = life outside work
● the other = work

這個 [we] 不是在指某一個小群體，
是有一種「包括作者和讀者」的 We !
英文裡有一種很常見的用法，叫做 inclusive we。
意思是：
● 作者把自己包括進去
● 同時也把讀者包括進去
● 用 [we] 來形成一種共同面對問題、共同反思的語氣
這裡的 [we] 就是這種用法。
因為作者不是在說：
● [they should be careful]
● [Gen Z should step back]
● [workers should step back]
● [employers should step back]
他說的是：
● [we should be careful]
● [we should step back]
● [we should move forward]
這表示作者在做的，不是指向某一方開火，
作者向 整體社會 發出一個共同思考的邀請
所以答案最穩陣一定是：
● people in general / all of us / the writer and readers / society in general

body: 這題其實不是普通「找先行詞」，而是看作者 stance 的 pronoun
題
很多 pronoun 題是很直接的：
● [John saw Mary and he smiled.]
問 [he] 指誰。
但這題不是那種單純找最近名詞的 reference 題。
它比較像是：
作者此刻選擇用 [we]，是想把誰拉進這個討論裡？
這是一種 stance / voice 題。
作者如果用 [they]，會把自己和讀者放在外面；
但他用 [we]，就是在說：
● 這不是別人的問題
● 不是某一代人的問題
● 不是單一群體的問題
● 而是我們大家都要一起想的問題
所以這一題的重點，其實是：
[we] = shared responsibility / shared reflection
這也是為甚麼答案不能太窄

為甚麼 (ii) 不能寫 [actual termination]？
這是很常見的錯誤。
原文有：
● [a path toward actual termination materializes]
所以很多學生會想：
「最後不是講 termination 嗎？那應該填這個吧。」
但這樣不對，因為題目問的是：[This has been labelled ...]
也就是要你寫 現象的名稱， 不是最後可能出現的 結果。
要分清楚三層：
1. 現象名稱
● quiet firing
2. 手法
● [cutting responsibilities]
● [denying promotions and raises]
3. 最後結果
● [actual termination]
所以如果你寫 [actual termination]，
你就把「結果」誤當成「標籤」。
這是這題典型的失誤!

所以答案最準確就是：
● the reputations of quiet quitters

先看 paragraph 7 的整體邏輯
第7段的關鍵部分是：
● [Borchers has encountered a new term quiet firing]
● [reputations suffer as a result of perceived apathy]
● [responsibilities are gradually diminished]
● [a path toward actual termination materializes]
● [Companies have always had subtle ways to nudge people out the door]
● [to make someone miserable enough to leave]
這一段其實是在講一個非常清楚的過程：
perceived apathy
→ employer responds negatively
→ responsibilities are cut
→ opportunities are denied
→ person is pushed out
→ this can end in actual dismissal
所以 paragraph 7 裡，和「結束某人受僱」有關的字眼其實不只一個。
但如果題目問的是：

● have the opportunity to change that organization

為甚麼不是 adaptable？
這是最常見錯誤. 很多學生會看到原文有：
● [made them so adaptable]
就直接想抄 [adaptable]。
但如果你放回題目，就會變成：
● [which proved to be adaptable to them in their studies ...]
這樣不通 Grammar
原因是：
● [adaptable] 是形容學生 themselves 的狀態
● 題目句型卻是要一個形容那些數位技能「對他們有甚麼作用」的字
也就是說：
原文：they became adaptable
題目：these skills proved to be helpful to them
所以不能只抄原字，要做意義轉換和詞性配合。

[separate their personhood from their jobs]
很多學生做到這裡就停了，只寫：
● positive = they can push back against workplace norms
這不算錯，但仍然可以更完整。
因為 paragraph 10 最後一句又說：
● [it has become clear to many that they need to separate their personhood
from their jobs.]
這句表面看起來像是後半的負面收尾，
但它其實也包含一個正面面向：
Gen Z 因為看清楚了工作與自我的糾纏問題，
所以更知道自己需要劃清界線。
也就是說，科技和數位思維不只是讓他們反抗 norms，
還讓他們更有意識地去思考：
● 我不應該把人身價值完全交給工作
● 我要把 [personhood] 和 [jobs] 分開
這和整篇 quiet quitting 的核心非常吻合。
所以如果要把正面答案答得成熟一點，最好寫成：
● technology helps Gen Z push back against workplace norms
and
● helps them realize the need to separate their personhood from their jobs

runs.text: 這是很常見的誤答方向。
● [these kids would get off TikTok and do their jobs]
所以有些學生會把 paragraph 10 的負面答案寫成：
● They spend too much time on social media.
● They are lazy because of phones.
paragraph 10 的 negative argument 很精準：
● [boundaries between the digital and real are blurred]
● [They have so thoroughly mixed work and self]
● [office life hits a more personal level]
也就是說，這裡的 negative 不在於「懶散」或「分心」:
科技令工作和人格更難分開，
所以現代職場對他們的壓力更深、更貼身。
這和「懶」完全不是同一件事!

為甚麼不是 C. Callum Borchers？
這是最容易混淆的一個。

● [reputations suffer]
● [responsibilities are gradually diminished]
● [actual termination materializes]

quiet quitting 對做這件事的人自己有甚麼壞處
而不是它怎樣影響同事和團隊。
所以：
● D = consequences spread outward to colleagues and teams
● C = consequences fall back on the quiet quitter himself/herself
這就是兩者的分別

先定義 [cynical] 在這題裡的意思
，[cynical] 比較接近：
● 冷嘲熱諷
● 對人不留情面地貶低
● 把一件事講得很不堪、很可笑、很低劣
● 帶有 contempt（不屑）和 mockery（嘲弄）

如果一個 comment 只是：
● 不同意
● 有保留
● 覺得現實上未必好
那未必算 cynical。

● 語氣刻薄
● 用很重、很誇張、很貶低的字

A 的 comment 是：
● [Figuring out how work fits into a life well lived is hard, but I think it’s
an evolution that has to happen. The question is what comes next.]
這句的語氣是甚麼？很明顯是：
● reflective（反思）
● thoughtful（思考式）
● open-minded（開放）
● calm（平靜）
他／她的意思是：
● 要弄清工作怎樣放進好好生活之中，確實不容易
● 但這種改變是必須發生的
● 真正的問題是：接下來會怎樣
這不是 cynical，因為它沒有：
● 嘲笑 quiet quitting
● 貶低做這件事的人
● 用侮辱性字眼
● 表現出 contempt
相反，A 幾乎是某程度上 理解 甚至 接受 這個變化。
為甚麼 A 不是答案？
因為 cynical 是「帶嘲諷和不信任的負面口氣」。
A 是很認真地在思考現象，不是挖苦
